title: The 147-file bug fix
intro: A three-line fix that cost a hundred and seventy thousand tokens to find. Step through the session and watch where the money actually goes.

provenance.source: the session is a narrated composite; steps 5-6 carry measured numbers, cited per step

foot: The measured version of this comparison is Capstone 2 · live_bench/SCENARIOS.md

steps.title: The ask — three lines, if you knew where they were
narrative: A developer asks their coding agent to fix a session-timeout bug in the authentication middleware. The fix will turn out to be three lines: one wrong comparison operator, plus a small test that pins it.

Nobody knows that yet — least of all the agent. Watch the context window on the right: right now it holds a system prompt, the tool definitions, and the question. That is the whole budget being spent on thinking.
steps.youDo: Ask for the fix the way you actually would — in one sentence, with no map attached.

terminal.text: sessions are timing out early — find and fix it in the auth middleware

middleware, then following whatever it depends on.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: 1% full. Every token in here is doing useful work.

steps.title: It starts reading
narrative: The agent greps, opens a file, finds an import, opens that one too. It reads the logging system. It reads the database migration history. It reads half the API endpoints. For reasons known only to itself, it reads the Terraform configs.

Every one of those was a reasonable guess. With no map of the codebase, following imports outward is the only search strategy available. Toggle Before / After to see what forty more file reads does to the window.
steps.claudeSays: Each read is cheap on its own — a few hundred to a few thousand tokens. It is the fan-out that costs, and the fan-out has no stopping rule.

steps.title: Escape at 147
narrative: The developer watches the file counter climb — 50, 90, 120 — and hits Escape at file 147. No fix, no diagnosis, and a bill.

The natural reaction is to blame the model: it's not smart enough to know where to look. Hold that thought for one more step, because the diagnosis is wrong and the wrongness is the whole point of this course.

items.label: exploration
items.note: finding things: greps, reads, and the transcript of both

steps.title: The diagnosis: no map, not low IQ
narrative: Look at what the agent read against what it needed. It was not being stupid; it was doing exactly what any competent newcomer does on their first day in an unfamiliar codebase — opening things to find out what they are.

A newcomer only does that once. They build a mental map and never pay the cost again. An agent starts every session at zero. That is the problem this course exists to solve: not a smarter model, a durable map.

steps.title: The same question, with a map
narrative: Now the measured version. On spring-framework — 9,195 Java files — we asked a mechanical benchmark the structural question an agent asks constantly: who calls this method?
Without a graph, answering for registerBeanDefinition means 174 file operations and 764,534 tokens of source. With a structural graph already built, it is one lookup returning all 1,037 callers.
Toggle Before / After. The reduction here is 93.9% — a 16.4× multiple — and it is the honest middle of the range, not the headline.
steps.youDo: Reproduce this yourself in Capstone 2: extract the graph, then run measure_tokens.py against your own repo.

steps.title: And the caveat that keeps you honest
narrative: That 16.4× is a mechanical measurement: whole-file reading versus one graph call. Real agents are cleverer than that — their grep returns matching lines, not whole files — so the live numbers are far less flattering.

Here is the same structural question run through actual agent sessions. The graph arm used more tokens than the baseline, because the agent still explored around the graph's answer. Below roughly 500 files, the tooling tax exceeds the savings entirely.

You will meet the full four-arm comparison in Capstone 2. For now, take the shape of the problem — most of your bill is exploration — and treat every published multiple with suspicion, including ours.

view.text: A map is not automatically cheaper — it is cheaper when the question is structural, the repo is large, and the agent is told to prefer the graph over grep. Getting those three conditions right is what the next thirteen modules are for.
